home.title: Three Body Problem
home.description: Explore the chaotic dynamics of three gravitational bodies in space.

info.title: About the Three-Body Problem
info.whatText: The three-body problem is a classic problem in classical mechanics that asks: given three celestial bodies with known masses, positions, and velocities, can we predict their future motion under mutual gravitational attraction?
info.chaosText: Unlike the two-body problem, the three-body problem has no general closed-form solution. The system is chaotic — tiny changes in initial conditions lead to dramatically different outcomes, making long-term prediction impossible.
info.historyText: First studied by Isaac Newton, the three-body problem has challenged physicists and mathematicians for centuries. Henri Poincaré discovered chaos theory while studying it. Today it remains relevant for orbital mechanics, astrophysics, and space mission planning.

timeline.title: Timeline of Solutions & Approaches
timeline.entry0d: Isaac Newton first posed the three-body problem in Principia, showing that even the Moon's orbit could not be fully explained by the Sun's and Earth's gravity alone.
timeline.entry1d: Leonhard Euler discovered the first particular solutions by assuming one body has negligible mass (the restricted three-body problem), laying groundwork for lunar theory.
timeline.entry2d: Joseph-Louis Lagrange found five equilibrium points (L1–L5) where a small body can remain stationary relative to two larger bodies. L4 and L5 are stable and host Trojan asteroids.
timeline.entry3d: Henri Poincaré proved that the three-body problem has no general analytic solution and discovered that even simple deterministic systems can exhibit unpredictable behavior — the birth of chaos theory.
timeline.entry4d: Karl Sundman found a convergent infinite series solution valid for all time (except collisions). While mathematically complete, the series converges too slowly for practical computation.
timeline.entry5d: The advent of computers enabled numerical integration methods (Runge-Kutta, symplectic integrators) allowing accurate simulations over limited time spans.
timeline.entry6d: Using variational methods, researchers discovered thousands of new periodic orbits — figure-eight, butterfly, and many other exotic trajectories.
timeline.entry7d: Modern ML techniques learn effective Hamiltonians and discover novel periodic orbits from data, pushing the boundary of what can be predicted in chaotic regimes.

newton.title: Newton's Formulation
newton.intro: In 1687, Isaac Newton published his magnum opus — Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy). In this work, he formulated the law of universal gravitation and the laws of motion, laying the foundations of classical mechanics. It is here that the three-body problem was first posed: Newton noticed that the gravitational interaction of three celestial bodies defies precise analytical description.
newton.lawText: At the core of Newton's formulation lies the law of universal gravitation. Two bodies with masses m₁ and m₂, separated by distance r, attract each other with a force:
newton.lawDetail: where G is the gravitational constant. The force acts along the line connecting the centers of mass of the two bodies.
newton.equationsText: For a system of N bodies, Newton's second law yields a system of differential equations:
newton.equationsDetail: For three bodies (i = 1,2,3) we obtain three second-order vector equations, equivalent to eighteen first-order scalar differential equations. This is the mathematical formulation of the three-body problem.
newton.systemText: Unlike the two-body problem, which has an elegant analytic solution (Kepler's laws), the three-body problem has no general closed-form solution. Newton understood this difficulty but lacked the analytical tools to overcome it. It would take over two centuries before Henri Poincaré proved that the three-body problem is generally non-integrable and exhibits chaotic behavior. This simulation uses the Euler method — the simplest numerical integration scheme, closest to Newton's original concept of motion under forces: acceleration is computed from force, then velocity is updated, followed by position.
newton.numericalText: For the two-body problem, Newton derived an exact analytical solution — Kepler's laws. Orbits are conic sections, and positions can be computed exactly at any time. For the three-body problem, no analytical solution exists, so the simulation uses 2 bodies with calculations following Kepler's laws. Let's examine a binary system of two equal-mass bodies on circular orbits: body 1 at (40, 0), m = 200; body 2 at (−40, 0), m = 200. G = 80.

euler.title: Euler's Solutions
euler.intro: In the 1760s, Leonhard Euler made the first serious attempt to solve the three-body problem after Newton's formulation. Euler introduced a crucial simplification — the restricted three-body problem, in which the mass of one body is negligible compared to the other two. This approximation proved extremely fruitful for celestial mechanics.
euler.restrictedText: Euler assumed that one of the three bodies has negligible mass (m₃ → 0) and does not affect the motion of the two massive bodies. The two massive bodies orbit their common center of mass following Kepler's laws, while the small body moves in their gravitational field. This simplification reduces the problem to the motion of a single body in a time-varying gravitational field.
euler.eulerMethodText: Euler also developed the simplest numerical integration method for ordinary differential equations (ODEs), now known as Euler's method. For an ODE system dy/dt = f(t, y), the method approximates the solution by moving forward along the tangent line given by the derivative f(t_n, y_n) at each point, using a fixed step size h.
euler.significanceText: Euler's work on the restricted three-body problem became the foundation for lunar theory and asteroid orbit calculations. His numerical integration method, though rarely used today in its pure form, remains the conceptual basis for more advanced methods. This simulation uses Euler's method as a tribute to his pioneering work.

lagrange.title: Lagrange Points
lagrange.intro: In 1772, Joseph-Louis Lagrange, while studying the restricted three-body problem, discovered five equilibrium points where the gravitational forces of two massive bodies balance the centrifugal force in the rotating reference frame.
lagrange.conceptText: In the rotating reference frame co-moving with two massive bodies, there are five points where a body of negligible mass can remain stationary relative to the massive bodies. At these points, the gravitational attraction of the massive bodies and the centrifugal force cancel each other out.
lagrange.collinearText: Three points lie on the line connecting the two massive bodies. L₁ is between the bodies, L₂ is beyond the smaller body, L₃ is beyond the larger body. All three are unstable: small perturbations cause the body to drift away. However, L₁ and L₂ are actively used for space missions (James Webb Telescope at L₂, SOHO at L₁).
lagrange.triangularText: Two points form equilateral triangles with the two massive bodies. L₄ lies 60° ahead of the smaller body in its orbit, L₅ 60° behind. When the mass ratio μ = m₂/(m₁ + m₂) < 0.0385, these points are stable. In the Solar System, this explains the Trojan asteroids — thousands of asteroids at the L₄ and L₅ points of the Jupiter—Sun system, as well as at other planets.
lagrange.significanceText: L₁ and L₂ are widely used for space observatories and probes due to their stable position relative to Earth and the Sun. The James Webb Space Telescope is at the Sun—Earth L₂ point. L₄ and L₅ are important for understanding Solar System dynamics and planetary system evolution.
lagrange.numericalTitle: Example: L₄ and L₅ in the Simulation
lagrange.numericalText: Consider a binary system with masses m₁ = 500 and m₂ = 10. The mass ratio of the smaller body to the total is μ = m₂/(m₁ + m₂) = 10/510 ≈ 0.02. For the triangular Lagrange points to be stable, μ must be less than 0.0385 (Routh's criterion); our value of 0.02 satisfies this condition. The distance between bodies is a = 60. poincare.title: Poincaré's Discoveries
poincare.intro: In 1887, King Oscar II of Sweden established a prize for solving the three-body problem. Poincaré submitted a memoir that initially contained an error — but correcting this error led to his greatest discovery. He proved that the three-body problem is generally unsolvable analytically and exhibits chaotic behavior: trajectories are extremely sensitive to initial conditions. His work laid the foundations of chaos theory.
poincare.chaosText: Poincaré showed that unless a three-body system is a special case (such as Lagrange's equilateral triangle or Euler's collinear configuration), its behavior is fundamentally unpredictable over long timescales. He discovered homoclinic intersections — structures where stable and unstable manifolds interweave, creating a complex web of trajectories.
poincare.significanceText: Poincaré's work on the three-body problem became the foundation of dynamical systems theory and chaos theory. His ideas found applications in physics, biology (population dynamics), economics (market cycles), and many other fields. The butterfly effect — a metaphor for sensitive dependence on initial conditions — was first described by Poincaré.
poincare.numericalText: Consider a configuration close to Lagrange's equilateral triangle: three equal-mass bodies (m = 100) at the vertices of a triangle with side ≈ 40. The bodies have circular velocities (v ≈ 14.14) for stable co-rotation, but body 3's velocity is perturbed by 10% along the X axis. This small deviation from the ideal configuration leads to chaos after several orbits — a vivid demonstration of sensitivity to initial conditions.

sundman.title: Sundman's Series
sundman.intro: In 1909–1912, Finnish mathematician Karl Sundman proved that the three-body problem admits an analytical solution in the form of convergent power series. His work represents the pinnacle of classical celestial mechanics, completing the search for an analytical solution begun by Newton.
sundman.theoremText: Sundman showed that the trajectories of three bodies can be represented by convergent power series in a regularized time variable s. The key idea is a time transformation dt = Ω(r) ds with a function Ω that vanishes at collisions. This removes the singularities from the differential equations, and the series converge for all real t.
sundman.regularizationText: The main difficulty is the singularity at collisions, when the denominator r_{ij} → 0. Levi-Civita proposed a coordinate transformation that unfolds the collision: a complex coordinate w = u + iv is introduced such that z = w², where z = x + iy is the relative position. This maps the collision point (z = 0) to a regular point (w = 0) and doubles angles — the collision becomes an ordinary passage through zero.
sundman.timeRegularizationText: Along with the coordinate transformation, Sundman used a change of the time variable dt = r ds, where r is the distance between the colliding bodies. This transformation slows down time near the collision, making the trajectory smooth in s.
sundman.analyticText: In the regularized variables (w, s), the equations of motion have no singularities. The solution can be analytically continued through the collision point — the trajectory is holomorphic (complex-analytic) in the vicinity of w = 0. The solution expands into a convergent Taylor series in w and s throughout the domain, except for isolated singular points.
sundman.seriesText: After regularization, the solution r_i(s) is represented by a power series with a nonzero radius of convergence R. The series converges on the entire real axis, but singular points in the complex plane limit the convergence rate. The coefficients behave as a_n ~ C·R⁻ⁿ·n^α. The radius R is so small that practical accuracy requires an astronomical number of terms.
sundman.convergenceRateText: The convergence rate is determined by the distance to the nearest singularity in the complex s-plane:
sundman.catchText: Computing one orbital period requires ~N = 10^(8·10⁶) terms. This number exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe. Sundman's series is a landmark theoretical result, demonstrating the gap between mathematical solvability and practical computability.
sundman.significanceText: Sundman completed the classical stage of the three-body problem investigation. An analytical solution exists, but his work revealed fundamental limitations: even when a solution exists, obtaining it in practice may require prohibitive resources — foreshadowing ideas in computational complexity theory.
sundman.numericalText: Two bodies of equal mass m = 100 fall toward each other along the X axis with initial velocity v₀ = 0, initial distance d = 20.
sundman.numericalRegText: A singularity occurs at x → 0. Apply 1D Levi-Civita regularization: x = u², dt = x ds. After substitution, we obtain the harmonic oscillator equation — regular at the collision point:
sundman.numericalRegText2: The equation is regular at u = 0. Solution: u(s) = A sin(ωs + φ), x(s) = u²(s) is analytic everywhere. The Taylor series for x(s) converges in the vicinity of s_collision — the collision has become a regular point.
sundman.numericalSeriesText: In regularized time s, the trajectory expands into a convergent series:
sundman.simulationText: Numerical integration (Velocity-Verlet) is a practical alternative to Sundman's prohibitively slow series.

numerical.title: Numerical Integration
numerical.intro: The three-body problem generally has no analytical solution, but it can be solved numerically — time is discretized and body positions are computed step by step.
numerical.eulerText:
The simplest numerical integration method. At each step, acceleration is assumed constant: position and velocity are updated along the tangent line to the true trajectory.

Local truncation error (per step) — O(h²), where h is the time step. Global error (after integrating over a fixed interval) — O(h). To halve the error, you must halve the step size. The method is not symplectic: energy monotonically increases over time, causing orbits to blow up.
numerical.rk4Text:
The classical fourth-order Runge-Kutta method. Each step computes four intermediate accelerations: at the start, at two trial midpoints, and at the end. These are then averaged with weights (1:2:2:1).

Local error — O(h⁵), global — O(h⁴). To halve the error, you need only reduce the step by ~16%. But the method is not symplectic: over long timescales, energy slowly drifts (usually downward). RK4 is a good choice for short intervals or when high per-step accuracy is needed.
numerical.verletText:
A second-order symplectic integrator. Unlike Euler and RK4, Velocity-Verlet preserves the geometric structure of phase space (the symplectic form).

«Symplectic» means the method conserves phase space volume — analogous to area preservation in phase space. In practice, this yields energy conservation over long timescales: energy does not systematically drift, but merely oscillates around the true value. The method is also time-reversible.

Velocity-Verlet is the gold standard for celestial mechanics. Its global error is O(h²), but due to its symplectic properties, it outperforms RK4 of the same order over intervals of thousands or millions of steps.
numerical.comparisonText: Euler's method accumulates error quickly and does not conserve energy. RK4 is accurate over short intervals but does not systematically conserve energy. Velocity-Verlet is the best choice for gravitational problems: it is symplectic (conserves phase space volume) and provides good energy conservation over long times.
numerical.simulationText: Switch the integration method and observe how well the orbit is preserved.
numerical.paramsIntro: A few words about our simulator and the challenge of orbit rendering: we are balancing accuracy and performance. Accuracy is determined by:
numerical.paramsMethod: integration method — Velocity-Verlet gives the best energy conservation, RK4 is a balance, Euler is the crudest
numerical.paramsSoft: — the smaller, the more accurate gravity at close distances
numerical.paramsPerformanceEnd: itself: the smaller the step or the more steps, the higher the CPU load.
numerical.paramsConclusion: Thus, the described integration methods at the accuracy settings used in the simulator provide orbit stability for approximately 3000 frames. Increasing accuracy further may cause the page to freeze (or perhaps you have already encountered this).

periodic.title: Periodic Orbits
periodic.intro: Despite the chaotic nature of the three-body problem, exact periodic solutions exist — orbits that repeat their trajectory after a fixed time interval. The main known families are listed below.
periodic.lagrangeText:
Stationary configurations where gravitational forces and centripetal acceleration balance each other.

L₁, L₂, L₃ (collinear points): lie on the line through the two massive bodies. Unstable, but used in space missions (James Webb telescope at L₂).

L₄, L₅ (triangular points): form equilateral triangles with the two massive bodies. Stable for mass ratio μ < 0.0385. Tadpole and horseshoe orbits exist around L₄ and L₅.
periodic.zeroMomentumText: A family discovered in the late 20th century. The system does not rotate as a whole — total angular momentum is zero. The most famous representative is the figure-eight orbit.
periodic.figure8Text: The most famous periodic solution, discovered by Moore (1993) and popularized by Chenciner and Montgomery (2000). Three equal-mass bodies trace a figure-eight trajectory, alternately catching up to each other. Period ~6.4 time units, stable to small perturbations.
periodic.suvakovText: In 2013, physicists Milovan Šuvakov and Veljko Dmitrašinović systematically explored the initial condition space and found new classes of periodic orbits with equal masses. The names describe the visual shape of the trajectory:
periodic.butterflyText: Butterfly I — the trajectory resembles butterfly wings. One of the most aesthetic solutions.
periodic.dragonflyText: Dragonfly — an elongated orbit with characteristic lateral wings.
periodic.mothText: Moth I—III — three varieties differing in the number of trajectory lobes.
periodic.gogglesText: Goggles — two symmetric loops connected by a bridge.
periodic.yinYangText: Yin-Yang — an orbit with inner and outer parts, resembling the yin-yang symbol.
periodic.bumblebeeText: Bumblebee — a chaotic-looking yet strictly periodic orbit with buzzing motion.
periodic.yarnText: Yarn — a complex intertwined trajectory resembling a ball of yarn.
periodic.hierarchicalText:
Sheen orbit families (2016): include ovals, ring shapes, and new topologies, including Yarn-ovals.

Shuttle-type orbits: one body oscillates back and forth between the other two, resembling a shuttle in a loom.

Animated examples of such complex systems can be found in scientific discussions (Reddit, arXiv).
periodic.restrictedText: When one body has negligible mass (satellite, asteroid), the problem reduces to the motion of a test particle in the field of two massive bodies.
periodic.lyapunovText: Planar periodic orbits around the L₁ and L₂ libration points. Used for spacecraft maneuvers.
periodic.haloText: Three-dimensional periodic orbits around L₁, L₂. The James Webb telescope is on a halo orbit around the Sun—Earth L₂ point.
periodic.lissajousText: Quasi-periodic orbits describing complex shapes resembling Lissajous curves — pendulum oscillations in different planes.
periodic.simulationText: Switch presets and integration methods to explore different periodic orbits.

homological.title: Homological Map
homological.intro: The homological (shape-space) approach classifies periodic three-body orbits by their topology on the shape sphere — a 2D sphere where each point corresponds to a triangle configuration of the three bodies, up to rotation and scaling.
homological.aaText: In Russian and astrophysical literature, the phrase “homology map” often refers to the work of T. A. Agekyan and J. P. Anosova. This is not a map of trajectories on the shape sphere, but a planar map of initial triangular configurations of three bodies after normalization by scale. It is especially important for the free-fall, or brake, problem: three equal masses start from rest, and their evolution reveals decay, binary formation, ejection of the third body, or a long-lived resonant interaction.
homological.aaConstructionText: Translation, rotation, and scale are removed first: the largest mutual separation is taken as the unit length. Two bodies are fixed on the X axis, for example at (0, 0) and (1, 0), and the third body is represented by a point (x, y). After using reflections and permutations of equal bodies, one keeps a fundamental domain: a shield-shaped region or one of its sectors. Each point in this domain is one similarity class of triangles, meaning one initial shape of the system.
homological.aaInterpretationText: In classical numerical experiments, every point of the map is integrated as a separate triple system. The color can encode lifetime before decay, which body escapes, which final binary forms, whether a collision occurs, or how reversible the motion is. Such maps show bands of fast escape, islands of long-lived resonances, and fractal boundaries between outcomes — a direct visual signature of chaos in the three-body problem.
homological.aaRelationText: The Agekyan — Anosova map and the shape sphere express the same reduction idea: a configuration is reduced to the shape of a triangle. They are used differently. The shape sphere is convenient for topology of periodic orbits and winding numbers around collision points. The Agekyan — Anosova map is convenient for scanning initial conditions: it turns a continuum of starting triangles into a two-dimensional diagram where stability and decay regions become visible.
homological.aaDiagramCaption: Homology map of the three-body free-fall problem. Colors encode the decay time of the system.
homological.shapeSphereText: The configuration of three bodies in the plane can be reduced to a single point on a 2-sphere, called the shape sphere. This reduction eliminates translations, rotations, and overall scaling, leaving only the intrinsic shape of the triangle formed by the bodies. The north and south poles correspond to equilateral triangles (Lagrange equilibria L₄ and L₅), and the equator contains three points where two bodies collide. Periodic orbits in real space become closed curves on this sphere.
homological.coordinatesText: To eliminate translations, introduce relative coordinates: η₁ = r₂ − r₁ and η₂ = r₃ − (m₁r₁ + m₂r₂)/(m₁ + m₂). The mass-weighted vector ρ = (η₁/√μ₁₂, η₂/√μ₁₂₃) lies in ℂ². Physical rotation corresponds to ρ → e^(iφ) ρ, and scaling to ρ → λρ. The true shape is therefore the quotient of ℂ² minus zero by ℂ* — the complex projective space ℂP¹ ≅ S², the shape sphere.
homological.coordinatesEquationText: Jacobi vectors and the Hopf map:
homological.hopfMapText: The reduction from ℂ² to S² is the famous Hopf fibration. Introducing coordinates z₁ = ρ₁ + iρ₂, z₂ = ρ₃ + iρ₄, every (z₁, z₂) ≠ (0, 0) defines a point on the Riemann sphere via the Hopf map. The sphere coordinates are (θ, φ), where the north pole (θ = 0) corresponds to the equilateral triangle with masses in cyclic order (Lagrange L₄), and the south pole (θ = π) to the reversed triangle (L₅). The equator (θ = π/2) contains all collinear configurations.
homological.collisionText: Three binary collisions (r₁₂ = 0, r₂₃ = 0, r₃₁ = 0) occupy fixed positions on the equator at φ = 0, 2π/3, 4π/3. On the shape sphere, these are punctures — points where the trajectory has a removable singularity if regularization is applied. The three collision points are all that remain of the Newtonian singularities after the reduction. Any orbit on the shape sphere that avoids these three points corresponds to a collision-free physical trajectory.
homological.collisionCoordsText: Collision point coordinates on the shape sphere:
homological.visualText: The canvas below shows the shape sphere. Colored curves represent periodic orbit families winding around the three collision points (marked in red). The legend shows the homology class (a, b, c) — winding numbers around each collision point.
homological.homologyTitle: Homology Classes — The Algebraic Topology of Orbits
homological.homologyText: On the 3-punctured sphere, the fundamental group π₁(S² \ (p₁, p₂, p₃)) is the free group on three generators g₁, g₂, g₃, where each gᵢ is a loop encircling collision point pᵢ. A periodic orbit defines a conjugacy class in this free group — its homotopy class. Abelianizing gives the first homology group H₁ = ℤ³, and the winding numbers (a, b, c) ∈ ℤ³ are the image of the orbit in this abelian group. Homotopy is stronger than homology: two orbits with the same winding numbers may be homotopically distinct (different word in the free group).
homological.homologyExampleText: The figure-8 orbit has homology class (1, 1, 1) — it winds once around each collision point. Butterfly I has (2, 1, 1). Different homology classes correspond to topologically distinct orbits that cannot be continuously deformed into each other without passing through a collision.
homological.classificationIntro: The 2013 work by Milovan Šuvakov and Veljko Dmitrašinović classified periodic three-body orbits into five classes based on their geometric and algebraic symmetries on the shape sphere:
homological.significanceText: The homological classification provides a complete topological taxonomy of periodic three-body orbits. It reveals that the seemingly endless variety of periodic orbits falls into a finite set of topological families. This approach connects the three-body problem to algebraic topology and has been extended to binary systems, hierarchical triples, and relativistic corrections.
homological.classDetailsText: The five symmetry classes are distinguished by how the orbit behaves under discrete symmetry operations on the shape sphere: reflection across a great circle (mirror symmetry) and central inversion (antipodal map).
homological.classIADetail: Two orthogonal reflection symmetries (D₂). The orbit's shape-sphere trace is invariant under two independent reflections across perpendicular great circles. This produces winding numbers (n, n, n) — equal around all three collision points. The figure-8 (1, 1, 1) and Bumblebee (3, 3, 3) are examples. The D₂ group is the largest possible symmetry for a three-body orbit.
homological.classIBDetail: One reflection + central symmetry (C₂ × Z₂). One plane of reflection is preserved, and the orbit is invariant under a 180° rotation in real space combined with time reversal (t → −t). On the shape sphere, this produces winding numbers where two collisions have the same count and the third is different. Butterfly I has (2, 1, 1); Moth I has (3, 1, 1).
homological.classIIADetail: Central symmetry only, type 1 (C₂-only). No reflection symmetry. The orbit has only the 180° rotation + time-reversal invariance. On the shape sphere, one collision point has winding number 0 — the orbit avoids it entirely. Butterfly II has (2, 2, 0).
homological.classIIBDetail: Central symmetry only, type 2 (C₂-only, different topology). Like II.A, only central symmetry, but all three winding numbers are non-zero. The path wraps around every collision point without any reflection plane. The Yarn orbit has (2, 3, 1).
homological.classIICDetail: Central symmetry only, type 3 (C₂-only, high winding). Central symmetry with larger winding numbers and no reflection symmetry. The Yin-Yang I orbit has (3, 5, 1); Yin-Yang II has (4, 5, 1). These are the most topologically complex discovered orbits in the planar equal-mass three-body problem.

ml.title: Machine Learning
ml.intro: Modern machine learning methods offer an alternative approach to the three-body problem: neural networks can predict trajectories without explicitly solving differential equations.
ml.approachText: A neural network is trained on numerical integration data: input is the initial positions and velocities, output is the positions after a given time interval. Once trained, the network can predict system evolution significantly faster than a classical integrator.
ml.limitsText: Neural networks generalize poorly to configurations not seen in the training data. Long-term prediction remains a challenge due to the chaotic nature of the system: error grows exponentially. A hybrid approach (ML for short intervals + numerical step for correction) is the most promising direction.
ml.simulationText: A trajectory that a neural network can learn to predict after training on Velocity-Verlet data.
